items.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998
items.q: Walter Cronkite was a jazz fan. Loved Wild Bill Davison. I still correspond with him.

ctx.x: Oh boy. He was a great band leader. He surrounded himself with great musicians. I don’t think he gave it that much thought but he actually was in the vanguard of breaking down racial barriers. At the same time that Benny Goodman was putting on his 1938 concert which had blacks and whites in the same band, Condon had his Town Hall concerts where he was doing the same thing. I think he just believed if you could play, you could play. Don’t worry about your sex, don’t worry about your color. I think he had — and…

personal life was in kind of a funny shambles. I mean it was sad, bittersweet, because he drank an awful lot but he loved to party, but he attracted to his club some of the world’s, I mean the great people of the world would come, the sports, they even some of them came into us, the carryover, the Condon’s that we ran. Walter Cronkite was a jazz fan. Loved Wild Bill Davison. I still correspond with him. So Condon was a very key person. I mean he grew up, he was born in Indiana and was in with those guys in…
And who was in your house band while you were there?
